(Today through Wednesday)...
Issued at 134 AM EDT Thu Oct 8 2026

Today Through Friday.

An upper-level shortwave trough tracking across the Upper Great 
Lakes has pushed dry surface boundary south across central Indiana 
over the last few hours with the wind direction now generally 
westerly to northwesterly across the forecast area. Diurnal heating 
will deepen the boundary layer to around 4kft, but weaker winds at 
the top of the boundary layer will keep wind gusts more towards 
15mph this afternoon and evening. Very dry mid-level air entraining 
into the boundary layer will cause minimum relative humidity values 
to drop into the 20 to 30 percent range during the afternoon. 
Combined with 10-hour fuel moisture values near 10 to 12 percent 
from antecedent dry conditions, slightly elevated fire weather 
danger is expected but the lighter winds will limit any higher-end 
impacts. High temperatures will top out in the upper 70s. High 
pressure building in behind the trough tonight will yield clear 
skies and light winds, favoring strong radiational cooling with 
overnight lows dropping into the upper 40s to low 50s.

On Friday, surface high pressure shifts eastward across the eastern 
Great Lakes, establishing a light easterly to southeasterly low-
level flow regime across the Ohio Valley. Model soundings from the 
GFS and ECMWF show persistent subsidence aloft keeping column 
moisture low, with PWATs under 0.60 inches. Mostly clear skies will 
allow afternoon highs to reach the mid 70s. Southeasterly return 
flow increases slightly Friday night as the surface high exits 
toward the Mid-Atlantic. Increasing upper-level cloudiness ahead of 
the approaching tropical system will keep Friday night lows slightly 
warmer, ranging from the upper 40s in the east to lower 50s in the 
west.

Saturday Through Wednesday.

Primary focus for the long term period centers on the interaction
between a Central Plains mid-level trough and tropical moisture 
associated with the remnants of Hurricane Isaias. Deterministic 
and ensemble guidance, including the GFS, ECMWF, GEFS, and EPS, 
demonstrate solid consensus in the remnants traveling north into 
the Ohio Valley bringing abundant tropical moisture both near the 
surface and aloft. High temperatures Saturday will reach the mid 
70s under thickening cloud cover. 

Precipitation will develop rapidly late Saturday evening and peak 
overnight into Sunday morning as strong isentropic lift is maximized 
beneath the right-rear quadrant of an accelerating Great Lakes jet 
streak. Dynamic cooling and widespread rainfall will keep Sunday 
high temperatures suppressed in the upper 60s, while elevated 
surface dewpoints hold Sunday night lows in the upper 50s.
Ensemble probabilities for 24-hour rainfall exceeding 0.75 inches
exceed 70 percent across central and southern Indiana, supporting
the potential for a 1.0 to 1.5 inch rainfall event if the track 
remains near to what the NHC is currently forecasting. There are 
some signs that the track may shift a bit to the southeast which 
will keep the axis of heavier rain focused closer to the Ohio 
River, but we continue to monitor the trends.

Rain will taper off from west to east Sunday evening as the tropical 
moisture core shifts toward the Mid-Atlantic and a mid-level dry 
slot moves in behind the exiting trough axis. Transient mid-level 
ridging and surface high pressure build in on Monday, allowing warm 
southwesterly flow to push high temperatures back into the upper 70s 
under mostly sunny skies.

By Tuesday and Wednesday, a deeper northern stream trough is 
forecast to amplify over the Great Lakes region, sweeping a strong 
cold front across central Indiana Tuesday. Cold air advection behind 
the boundary will bring temperatures closer to normal by Wednesday. 
Confidence on any precipitation with this frontal passage remains 
fairly low with only modest forcing with the system.
